demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one. Snake-related and pregnancy/birth reminders imply trauma contexts unrelated to bereavement, and there is no supporting threat or memory content linking them to this loss.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons similarly implies a trauma context involving violence, combat, or armed threat, which is unsupported by the stated trauma type and by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to justify unless the death specifically involved childbirth or infant loss; nothing else in the profile supports that context. This makes the trigger clinically implausible relative to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons implies a trauma context involving combat, assault, or armed responders. That does not fit the rest of this bereavement-focused profile and is not supported by the other trigger, threat, or strategy items, so it appears incoherent with the trauma type and overall formulation.

vignette: Rohan's eyes would often glaze over when he thought about his younger brother, Kumar, who had passed away suddenly three years ago. It was as if he was right back in that hospital room, feeling the same numbness and disbelieving horror. The anniversary of Kumar's death was approaching, and Rohan could feel the familiar dread creeping up on him. He had been dreading this day for weeks, mentally rehearsing all the terrible things that could happen to his loved ones, as if preparing himself for another tragedy would somehow make it more bearable. Rohan's wife, Nalini, had tried to be supportive, but he knew she was getting frustrated with his increasing irritability. He would lash out at her over small things, and then immediately regret it. His body seemed to react before his mind could catch up, leaving him feeling like a ticking time bomb. At work, he struggled to concentrate on his interior design projects, finding himself zoning out in the middle of meetings or snapping at colleagues. Rohan had been avoiding anything that reminded him of Kumar's passing, including funerals and cemeteries. He wouldn't even drive by the cemetery where Kumar was buried, taking a detour every time he needed to go to his parents' house. Talking about loss with others made him anxious, as if sharing their grief would somehow unleash his own pent-up emotions. When friends or family members tried to discuss their experiences of losing loved ones, Rohan would politely excuse himself, feeling like he was on the verge of unraveling. At home, Rohan's avoidance behaviors had taken a toll on his relationship with Nalini. They used to love hosting dinner parties and game nights, but now Rohan found excuses to avoid social gatherings, fearing that someone might bring up Kumar or ask about their family. He knew Nalini felt isolated and alone in her grief, but he couldn't seem to shake off the feeling of impending doom. As the anniversary approached, Rohan's flashbacks became more frequent. He would be working on a design project when suddenly, he was back in that hospital room, reliving the moment when the doctor delivered the news about Kumar's passing. His heart racing, his palms sweating, Rohan felt like he was living in a constant state of hypervigilance. It wasn't until Nalini sat him down and told him she couldn't take it anymore – that she needed her husband back – that Rohan realized he needed help. He was exhausted from trying to control his emotions, from avoiding anything that reminded him of Kumar's passing. For the first time in years, Rohan felt a glimmer of hope that maybe, just maybe, he could learn to live with his grief instead of letting it consume him. As he sat in the therapist's office, Rohan knew what brought him there: the desperate desire to break free from the suffocating grip of his memories and find a way to honor Kumar's memory without losing himself.
